newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Investment banks tip Philippine credit upgrade.
newsitem.headline: Investment banks tip Philippine credit upgrade.

text.p: The Philippines is ripe for another credit upgrade by major international rating agencies next year, two overseas investment banks have said.

In two separate reports, Merrill Lynch and Bankers Trust Research said the Philippines stood a very good chance for a sovereign rating upgrade to BB plus from BB. BB plus is the highest non-investment grade.
The country was upgraded by Moody's Investors Service and Standard and Poor's Ratings Group to BB from BB minus in May 1995 because of strong economic growth for three straight years.

In a paper released at a news conference on Monday, Merrill Lynch said: "Of the 18 emerging markets sovereign credits that are rated in the double B range ... We believe that the Republic of the Philppines is the leading candidate for a credit ratings upgrade on the basis of improvements in key economic ratios."

The paper by Joyce Chang and William Belchere of Merrill Lynch's global fixed-income research group predicted the country would be upgraded to an investment grade, triple B minus, by June 1998 when a new administration is set to take office.
President Fidel Ramos' term ends then and a new government is expected to be in place by June, 1998.
A rating upgrade would significantly reduce interest expenses and open up other markets to domestic borrowers.

Chang told reporters that most investors were already pricing Philippine debt papers as on par with investment grade papers. Since the beginning of the year, Philippine corporations have raised more than $1.5 billion in the international debt market.

"Despite the higher level of debt issuance this year compared to other years, the Philippines has been able to borrow at levels well below the average spread at issue of emerging markets debt of 284 basis points (above the equivalent U.S. treasury)," the Merrill report said.
The average interest rate of Philippine debt papers has been down at 150 to 250 basis points above the equivalent U.S. treasury from 250 to 375 basis points between 1993 and 1995.
Chang said critical ratios observed by credit agencies had also improved compared to other economies.

The Philippines' debt/exports ratio was at 135 percent of exports in 1995, lower than that of investment grade-rated Indonesia which was at 201 percent; Greece was at 283 percent; Colombia, 164 percent and India, 243 percent.
The Philippines also had one of the lowest debt-servicing ratios, which was at 16 percent of export earnings last year down from about 36 percent in the past.
